blurb: Constitutional jurisprudence, fundamental rights rulings, and doctrines established by the Supreme Court of India.

topics.title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) and the Basic Structure Doctrine
topics.hook: Decided by a 13-judge bench by a 7-6 majority on 24 April 1973, establishing that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution under Article 368.
topics.story:
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru, head of the Edneer Mutt in Kerala, challenged the Kerala government's land reform acts under Article 26 (right to manage religiously owned property). The Supreme Court convened its largest-ever bench of 13 judges to review earlier judgments in Shankari Prasad (1951), Sajjan Singh (1965), and Golaknath (1967).

By a narrow 7-6 majority, Chief Justice S.M. Sikri and six other judges held that while Parliament has wide amending powers under Article 368, it cannot amend or alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution. Chief Justice Sikri enumerated elements of basic structure including supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secular character, separation of powers, and federal character.

Justice H.R. Khanna provided the decisive vote, holding that 'amendment' implies preservation of the original entity's basic identity rather than its destruction. The judgment upheld the 24th Amendment (affirming Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights) but struck down part of Article 31C added by the 25th Amendment that excluded judicial review.

topics.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) and Due Process under Article 21
topics.hook: Expanded Article 21 from mere protection against executive action to require procedure established by law to be just, fair, and reasonable.
topics.story:
In 1977, the Janata Party government impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967, 'in the public interest', giving no reason. Maneka Gandhi challenged this under Article 32.

A 7-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that the right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21, overruling AK Gopalan (1950). Justice P.N. Bhagwati articulated that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive; it must satisfy the test of reasonableness and comply with natural justice.

This verdict interlocked Articles 14, 19, and 21 as a 'Golden Triangle', requiring any law depriving personal liberty to pass all three articles.

topics.title: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and Right to Privacy
topics.hook: Unanimous 9-judge bench verdict holding Right to Privacy as an intrinsic part of right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
topics.story:
Retired High Court Judge K.S. Puttaswamy challenged the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar scheme. The Union government argued Privacy was not a fundamental right, citing M.P. Sharma (1954, 8 judges) and Kharak Singh (1962, 6 judges).

A 9-judge Constitutional Bench unanimously declared Right to Privacy a fundamental right protected under Part III of the Constitution, overruling M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held privacy was not protected.

Justice D.Y. Chandrachud authored the lead judgment for four judges, establishing a three-fold test for state intrusion into privacy: legality (backed by law), necessity (legitimate state aim), and proportionality.
topics.why: CLAT questions focus on 9-judge bench ratio (9-0), Justice Chandrachud's proportionality test, overruled cases, and privacy as Article 21 right.

topics.title: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) and President's Rule under Article 356
topics.hook: A 9-judge bench ruled that President's rule under Article 356 is subject to judicial review and floor test is the mandatory method to prove majority.
topics.story: S.R. Bommai's Janata Dal government in Karnataka was dismissed in 1989 under Article 356 without a floor test. The 9-judge bench held federalism and secularism are basic structure elements. Dissolution of state assembly before Parliamentary approval is illegal.

topics.title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) - Decriminalisation of Section 377
topics.hook: Unanimous 5-judge bench strikes down 157-year-old Section 377 IPC to the extent it criminalised consensual adult LGBTQ intimacy.
topics.story: Overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013). Bench comprising CJI Dipak Misra, Justices R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, and Indu Malhotra held Section 377 violated Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21.

passages.title: The Basic Structure Doctrine
passages.passage: In April 1973, a thirteen-judge bench of the Supreme Court delivered a landmark judgment in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala. By a narrow margin of seven to six, the Court ruled that while Parliament possesses broad authority under Article 368 to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, this amending power is bounded. It cannot alter or destroy the basic structure or framework of the Constitution. Chief Justice S.M. Sikri and Justice H.R. Khanna observed that amendment implies variation without loss of identity. This verdict effectively overruled the rigid embargo laid down in Golaknath (1967) while preventing Parliament from becoming a constituent assembly.
